#8593. Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more important stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.)

The benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

You will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”

Well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand new city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

And sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next big upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.)

With a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

It’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

Another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

* Despite my positive raving about this neighborhood, I have no financial or business connection with the project or any of the team members. I am just really excited about their work and want them to succeed!

Damn that is exciting! Pedestrianism FTW!

I couldn’t agree more. This would create more beautiful, spacious, and healthy living spaces for everyone. While some may resist change, the benefits of building cities around people instead of cars are too significant to ignore.

Yay! I’m thrilled to read about a city of the future, and I look forward to hearing more when you spend the winter there. I gave them my email address so I could hear more in the future.

I’m an American attending a university in Sweden, and the city where I live is designed very similarly to what you describe. I live in a student apartment building which has 0 car parking spaces but an indoor bike parking room that accommodates about 50 bikes. Mostly because of distances, I’d say. The US are huge compared to Europe (and still mostly empty – to the point that cities spread horizontally to infinity rather than vertically – except San Francisco and Manhattan that are peninsulas).

In Europe, streets have always been very narrow because initially built just for humans and horses. This makes Europe perfect for biking + walking only. The countries and cities are much smaller, too. And since the population density is also way higher in Europe, they have all incentives to keep it human-friendly.

Also, the US are the 3rd oil producer in the world. Europe, with the exception for Norway, has little to no oil. In other words, the US were incentivized to push for oil consumption (good for the economy – with a 1900s mindset obviously). Europe, not so much, since oil is imported and as a result more expensive.

One major improvement in places like Phoenix and Las Vegas versus the rest of the country is that they have managed to mostly eliminate suburban lawns. It’s 50 years since the original movie captured our hearts and fighting spirit in 1976, but the movie’s motivating message; that we can all push ourselves to be more than we thought we could, is still as relevant today as it ever was. With more than 40,000 runners expected to descend in Philadelphia, each of the three Rocky Run categories have sold out.

The first official Rocky Run began in 2014 with heavyweight beginnings, attracting 7,000 runners, but it has gone from strength to strength since. And, while organizers had expected around 30,000 competitors to descend in Philly this year, the final number will clock in at an incredible 40,000.

Those who are ready and set for November 14, 2026, have a choice of three categories, catering to different abilities, so that anyone can “Go For it.”

The half marathon actually combines the 5K and 10-mile runs, meeting the 13.1-mile requirement, and besides channeling your inner Rocky Balboa and going the distance, there are cool medals to be won. The 5K finisher medal celebrates 50 years of Rocky, while the 10-mile finisher medal depicts The Italian Stallion’s triumphant celebration at the top of the famous steps leading up to the Philadelphia Museum of Art. The 13.1-mile finishers is a large, heavyweight design that has “50” emblazoned on one side, while the other side has a vintage image of Rocky in training.

In addition to the Rocky Run, Philadelphia continues to show its love for the most famous fictional boxer in history. The city held its first “Rocky Day,” on December 3, 2023. No doubt, the inspirational story of one man going the distance continues to resonate around the world.

“Once again it’s a magical time of the year, The Rocky Run,” said Stallone in a recent social media post to promote the activities on November 14. Of course, Sly has been heavily active during Rocky’s 50th celebrations. He released his appropriately titled autobiography, “The Steps” and even brought back the man behind Rocky’s signature soundtrack, Bill Conti, for a live concert in New York to go along with a screening of the film. And for those, who still can’t get enough of Sylvester Stallone’s creation, the story of how a struggling actor defied the odds to become the star of one of cinema’s most successful franchises is also set to hit theaters, with “I Play Rocky” starring Anthony Ippolito as the struggling boxer given a once in a lifetime shot, and Stephan James playing Apollo Creed.

As to whether Sly will make an appearance at this record-breaking Rocky Run, fans are certainly hoping that Philadelphia’s favorite son will tread his old stomping ground once again.

#8591. After a Decade of Refusing to Use a Treadmill, I Finally Gave In. Here’s How It’s Making Me a Better Runner.

Cold, dark days don’t have to derail your running. The treadmill might be the fix you need.

When the weather dipped below freezing for the first time last winter and the sun began to set at 4:30 p.m., I knew I’d have to leave my typical after-work miles behind. Cold weather and early darkness have always been an easy one-two punch to my running motivation.

I’d also long held another line in the sand: I didn’t run on treadmills—at least not since high school gym class. I took to calling myself a “purist” because I didn’t think running was worth it if it wasn’t outside in nature. I believed my cause was noble, but really, I was just piling up excuses not to run in the winter.

So I decided to give treadmill running a chance. I set out to complete one to two easy runs per week for a month to see if it could help me stay consistent through the winter. Within a few weeks, I was running more than I ever had in winters past—and reconsidering what held me back all those years.

My experiment started after work in late fall. I turned to one of the Bowflex treadmills we have at Runner’s World headquarters. Earlier in the day, my editor casually mentioned that my Apple Watch would sync directly to the treadmill for a more accurate reading, a suggestion that made me more excited to get started on my test.

I walked up to the treadmill and the first thing I noticed was that if I wanted to, I could put my Netflix password into the built-in monitor and fire up an episode of Brooklyn Nine-Nine for the 200th time. While this capability isn’t very advanced as far as treadmill features go nowadays, the shift from the bare-bones experience I remembered from a decade ago in high school gym class amazed me.

I decided to go simple for my first run, tapping in with my Apple Watch and committing to a 30-minute easy effort with just a podcast to entertain me.

The run itself was good, but left me puzzled. I immediately focused on how each foot strike offered a different sensation than I was used to outside. After a minute of adjusting the belt speed, I settled into a pace that felt similar to my outdoor easy runs. What I found, though, was that the treadmill speed read a completely different pace than my outdoor runs.

After 30 minutes at zero incline, I completed just 2.56 miles at an 11:51 pace with my heart rate right at my usual 150 beats per minute (bpm). That 11:51 average was nearly two minutes slower than my outdoor 10:00 easy pace, but I felt like I was right at my normal outdoor effort level.

Still, I walked away encouraged. I logged a run, avoided the weather, and felt great doing it.

My experiment continued with more 30-minute easy runs over the next couple of weeks. Each one raised the same question: Why did an effort that felt identical to my normal 10:00 outdoor easy runs translate to a treadmill pace of well over 11:00 per mile? Adding to the confusion, I got a new watch (the Coros Pace 4), and it consistently recorded slightly longer distances than the treadmill itself displayed.

After my third run, I brought all my questions to a chat with Birmingham-based RRCA level II- and USATF-certified run coach Alex Morrow, founder of Resolute Running. I described to him how, on the treadmill, I felt I was giving a similar effort compared with my outdoor runs, but was running at a significantly slower pace, and I asked him why he thought this was the case.

“When you’re outside and you’re running at an easy pace, you’re looking at the trees, you’re waving at other runners, and your mind gets to dissociate from what you’re doing,” Morrow says. “When you’re on a treadmill, there’s very little stimulation,” beyond your body moving.

Because I’d been running exclusively outdoors since high school, I was used to looking around at the cars as they passed by, the birds in the air, and any number of distractions along my route. As soon as I hopped on the treadmill, though, none of that was there to capture my attention. Right away, I locked in on the difference in every step, and became consumed by how far off my pace ended up being from what I expected.

Changing a long-held belief is tough, especially when it’s rooted in identity. “It’s like turning a battleship around,” says Morrow. “It takes time and it’s never easy.” In my case, the belief that “real runners” don’t use treadmills stuck around for years.

Once I started running on one, though, I accepted it as a suitable tool for consistent running almost immediately. The hardest part of flipping my mindset wasn’t logging the miles or dealing with boredom, it was simply stepping onto the belt in the first place.

If you’re new to treadmill running, or have avoided it for the same reasons I did, my best advice is to try it with an open mind. Don’t worry if your pace looks slower than what you’re used to seeing outside. That mental hurdle of mine ended up not really mattering much. I let effort guide my runs, my podcasts entertain me, and I judge my success based on time on feet rather than actual miles.

My biggest takeaway from the experience was consistency. According to Morrow, that’s where treadmill running becomes one of the most powerful tools a runner can use, especially in the winter.

Through my trial efforts, I realized I wasn’t frustrated with the treadmill itself, I was simply focused on learning more about my running. Curiosity helped me keep a steady schedule, and in just a few weeks, I’d already run more in the winter than I had in years.

“Consistency is so much more important than having one killer workout,” Morrow explains. “I would much rather you have four or five average workouts than three killer workouts.” This idea counters how a lot of runners think about training, especially when motivation dips. It’s flashy to chase breakthrough days in perfect conditions, but you build fitness by stacking days together, even when the circumstances aren’t ideal.

For runners who live in areas heavily impacted by harsh winter weather, the treadmill is a saving grace. “Something is always better than nothing,” Morrow says. “Jogging three miles on a treadmill is better than skipping your workout completely because it’s cold outside.”

When weather threatens to derail a week of training, the opportunity that a treadmill provides becomes crucial to your development as a runner. “Consistency creates physiological adaptations in your body that allow you to reach your goals,” Morrow says. Those adaptations include a boost in aerobic fitness development, running economy, VO2 max, and lactate threshold, he continues. It’s adaptations like these that establish an excellent fitness base for marathon training.

Looking back on my career as a recreational runner, my biggest mistake wasn’t refusing to run on the treadmill; it was letting that ignorance cost me months of consistent running every year. Now, the excuses that held me back are gone. I’ve continued using the treadmill to not only knock out frequent easy runs but conquer the occasional interval workout or speed session.

Matt Rudisill is an Associate Service Editor who has been with Runner's World since 2025. A Nittany Lion through-and-through, Matt graduated from Penn State in 2022 with a degree in journalism and worked in communications for the university's athletic department for three years as the main contact and photographer for its nationally-ranked cross country and track & field teams. Matt was also heavily involved in communications efforts for Penn State football, men's basketball, and women's gymnastics. In his role with Runner's World, Matt has interviewed Olympians, world champions, and countless experts in the field to create service content that helps runners of all ages and experience levels train smarter and race faster. When he’s not out jogging, Matt can be found tweeting bad takes about the Phillies or watching movies.

#8590. Robert Strauss Has the Full-Body F45 Workout to Stay Fit over 40

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

As the General Manager of WWE’s NXT brand, a pro wrestling coach, and the owner of eight gyms across Florida, Robert Strauss understands the importance of rapid workouts to stay ripped. To that end, the man known to millions of WWE fans as “Robert Stone,” says that F45 workouts are perfect for staying fighting fit, and he proved it with a dedicated demonstration for M&F.

The F45 concept sees gym goers from all over the world following the same daily workout. “Everybody does the same workout every day, and you’re never going to do the same workout twice,” says Strauss. “It’s a 45-minute workout that includes your warmup, your workout, and your cooldown.”

Indeed, F45 workouts tackle fitness from all angles. There are focused cardio days, strength days, and hybrid days to keep each session stimulating. And, there’s often a choice of two different exercises as you move through the circuit. “So, you really can get a full body workout in, any day that you come into an F45, and you’re always going to leave drenched in sweat, I promise you that,” adds the NXT GM.

F45 sessions begin as soon as the clock activates and include short demonstrations followed by a guided warmup with dynamic stretching, to prepare yourself for the pump ahead. Then, after the main session is done, there’s a cooldown period before you tackle the rest of the day, feeling ready to bodyslam the world.

Greeting us at his Baldwin Park, FL, location, Strauss, who is the father of twin boys, explained that F45 has provided structure so that he can keep up with the next generation at both at home and in NXT. He completed the following session between duties, proving that he hasn’t missed a beat.

(In this class, there were 4 minutes for setup)

Execute each exercise for 45 seconds.Rest and transition to the next exercise for 15 seconds.

High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) sessions such as this one can easily burn more than 500 calories in 45 minutes, depending on the effort put in, and you’ll supercharge your fat burning power with Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption (EPOC) for the rest of the day.

You won’t need to walk around a vast gym space to hit all of the muscle groups either, because you’ll be completing each station while staying pretty much on the spot. This particular workout offered back and core strengthening exercises like crunches and rows, upper body testers like presses and extensions, and movements that also build the lower body with sumo stances and lying leg raises.

“One of the most inspiring things about NXT is that most of the trainees there are half my age,” says Strauss of his motivation to maintain muscle. “They are all phenomenal athletes that come from all over the world, and they are in the greatest shape. So, seeing them inspires me to continue my fitness journey. Also, I’m a twin dad to 10-year-olds, and I want to inspire them the way NXT Superstars inspire me. I want to inspire my kids so that they see their daddy is fit, and they want to be fit. It’s an important part of life for your mental and physical well-being,”

You can catch Strauss in his role as General Manager Robert Stone, stamping his authority on NXT, every Tuesday night on the CW Network in the U.S. and streaming internationally on Netflix.

#8589. The Best Smith Machine for Your Home Gym in 2025

The Smith machine sometimes gets a bad rap, but it can be a solid addition to any home gym.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Nov 2, 2026

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Other than the almighty treadmill, there may not be a piece of equipment more synonymous with commercial gyms than the Smith machine. Boasting tremendous versatility and functionality, this muscle-building tool is popular among lifters of all experience levels.

However, you don’t need a gym membership to enjoy its benefits. While it may have not been a home gym staple years ago, the Smith machine has become a must-have for many fitness enthusiasts. Offering added protection without a spotter for your bench presses, back squats, deadlifts, and other strength exercises, the Smith machine is a wise investment for those trying to build the ultimate garage gym.

With options spanning from traditional Smith machines to all-in-one home gym solutions, you might feel a bit overwhelmed about which direction to go. Luckily for you, our team of expert product testers did all the due diligence necessary to separate the cream from the crop. From analyzing the build materials to testing the smoothness of the bar path to assessing the value, we took the time to dissect each element in order to narrow down our list to just five.

In addition, we got some valuable insight from Mauro S. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness, on the benefits and what factors to consider when you’re shopping for a Smith machine.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If you’re searching for a multifunctional Smith machine that’s compatible with a ton of attachments, the Force USA G15 is the machine that can truly do it all — albeit at an expensive price point of around $5,500. However, there’s a reason it earned 4.5 out of 5 stars for versatility from our top product tester: you can perform a wide variety of exercises by taking advantage of all of its functionality.

Tipping the scales at nearly 1,000 pounds, the G15 combines a functional trainer, half rack, and Smith machine into a single, sturdy unit. Measuring over 6 feet wide, over 4 feet deep, and about 7 feet tall, the G15 earns a 4-star footprint rating. While there are more compact options, it’s still a good option for folks with limited space, especially considering the versatility you get.

Offering dual 289-pound weight stacks that keep it well-anchored, the G15 also scores 4 out of 5 stars for durability and construction.

“This thing is like a tank,” our tester says. “Once it’s assembled, it’ll basically be stuck in place.”

Unfortunately, our tester wasn’t as impressed with the cable pulley material. Asthey’re made from nylon instead of aluminum, they don’t move as smoothly and won’t be as durable as their metal counterparts.

Something that separates the G15 from many competitors is its ability to go from a 2:1 or 4:1 pulley ratio. This gives you the ability to make the weight feel like half or a quarter of the actual weight. While our tester would prefer a 1:1 ratio for more effective resistance, he says the 2:1 or 4:1 ratios “will be adequate for most people working out from home.”

The G15 comes with a lengthy list of attachments, including J-hooks, safety spotter arms, multi-grip dip handles, a multi-grip pull-up bar, band pegs, and a low row footplate. If you want to unlock even more training possibilities, the $700 G15 Upgrade Kit includes three additional strength training stations, three functional attachments, a TV mount, and four storage shelves.

Two knocks against this ultra-versatile machine: assembly and value.

Although some of the parts arrive pre-assembled, our assembly expert recommends budgeting “at least 20 man hours” to get the G15 fully put together. And if you want to leave it to the professionals, you’ll need to pay an additional $800.

At nearly $6,000 on its own, the G15 certainly isn’t made for budget-conscious shoppers. Our top product tester gave it 3.5 out of 5 stars for value, noting that Force USA could use better quality components, cables, and accessories, including one of the key parts of this premium-priced unit: the built-in barbell.“The knurling is super passive and not going to allow for an adequate grip for the user if you were to go heavy on any Smith machine movements,” he explains.

Want to crush a full-body workout with a single piece of equipment? The Titan Fitness Smith Machine can be the all-in-one solution that allows you to train your upper body, lower body, and core in a safe, effective manner.

Is it as versatile as the G15? No. Is it far more affordable? Yes.

For less than a third of the price, you can still get an excellent workout experience from the $1,7000 Titan Smith Machine. One of our more seasoned product testers used it for a variety of strength training sessions, highlighting how impressed she was by the smooth glide of the barbell and the angled design. In addition, this Smith machine is counterbalanced so you don’t have to support the entire 45-pound barbell like you do on other machines. Beginners will appreciate this, as the bar only feels like 15 pounds.

Unfortunately, like Force USA, Titan left our team wanting more out of the knurling.

“It’s fine for a Smith machine, but it’s definitely not the most grippy bar,” our tester says.

On the other hand, this machine earns high marks for its ergonomics. Our tester rated it 4 out of 5 stars in this category. She found the single-axis, angled design helped improve her muscle activation during lower-body weight training exercises like Smith machine squats and lunges.

Most importantly, she felt completely secure using this Titan machine. Not only was there no wobbling or shaking, but the bar moved smoothly, leading her to give a 5-out-of-5 rating for stability.

“This is a super stable machine; there was no give to it even when we were using heavy weights,” our tester says. “This was ultra-smooth.” While Titan priced this machine fairly, we’d like to see a better warranty. A one-year policy falls well short of what we expect from most brands. Plus, if you want to return a piece of equipment, you must pay the return shipping costs and a 20% restocking fee. That results in a disappointing customer experience score of just 2 out of 5 stars.

Don’t want a standalone Smith machine? Bolt Fitness has a space-saving solution in the form of the Storm Series Stinger Smith Machine Attachment. Compatible with any 3” x 3” frame using 1” hardware, this universal attachment can seamlessly integrate with your existing squat or power rack, opening the door to even more training possibilities.

We rate this Smith machine attachment a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers 12 different positions totaling 60” of vertical adjustments. That means you can quickly go from a steep incline bench press to a Romanian deadlift, making your workouts more efficient, too. Plus, we also like that this attachment has a 43” built-in multi-grip pull-up bar, giving you the ability to develop your vertical pulling strength and endurance.

Bolt also earns solid marks for construction, earning 4 out of 5 stars in this key category. However, our chief product tester warns not to expect quite the same level of craftsmanship as some better-known brands.

“You won’t see the same quality welds or powder coats from Bolt as you will from Rogue or REP,” he says.

Like several other nominees on this list, our tester was also disappointed with the Smith bar’s knurling. The passive knurl pattern won’t give you a particularly stable grip, especially when using heavier weights.

“You definitely won’t mistake this for an Olympic barbell,” our tester says.

As for the price? At around $1,100 this is on the expensive side for a Smith machine attachment. For example, the Bells of Steel Smith Machine Rack Attachment is much more affordable at $800. We rate it a 3 out of 5 for value, especially since you already need a rack to use it. Otherwise, expect to invest a significant chunk of change to get a fully functioning setup.

Just because you can’t afford to splurge on something like the G15 doesn’t mean you can’t find a Smith machine that fits within your budget. If you don’t have a ton of financial wiggle room, the RitFit Smith Machine is the most affordable option that earned our stamp of approval.

As our top product tester puts it, “If you’re looking for a Smith machine and you’re on an ultra-budget, this is it.”

At about $500 on Amazon, this machine is less than a third of the price of the Titan Fitness Smith Machine and less than a tenth of the cost of the G15. Of course, it’s not the most durable option on the market, but it offers sufficient versatility at a very attractive price point to earn a near-perfect value rating of 4.5 out of 5 stars.

Dubbed the “sleeper pick” by our tester, he notes that “the low price covers so many sins.”

Before we dive into some of RitFit’s shortcomings, let’s highlight some of the strengths of this machine. First, we rated it 4 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers built-in low row and lat pulldown capabilities using a plate-loaded cable pulley system that holds 165 pounds. The RitFit Smith Machine also comes with several attachments, including a pin-on landmine row and two multi-purpose pull-up handles.

Secondly, it has a compact design that makes it suitable for home gym setups with limited  space. It also weighs just 140 pounds, making it easier to move than other options on this list.

However, our tester had several callouts about the RitFit Smith Machine that deserve mentioning. With cheaper build materials and a lightweight design, it didn’t prove to be as stable as he would have liked, earning just 3.5 out of 5 stars for both construction and stability. Needless to say, this isn’t the best option if you want to lift heavy weights. Still, considering you could pay around the same price for a high-quality Olympic barbell, the RitFit Smith Machine is a solid option if you’re on a limited budget.

Imagine if you could turn your squat rack into a Smith machine in a matter of minutes. That dream can be a reality if you’re willing to invest around $700 on the VTS Lite Rack Attachment from Bulletproof Fitness, a lesser-known fitness equipment manufacturer that’s caught our attention.

While we haven’t gotten our hands on this attachment just yet, it’s hard not to get excited about the concept and execution by Bulletproof. The Versa Trolley System (VTS) Lite allows you to convert your squat rack into a Smith machine using your own barbell. The rollers are made from UHMW plastic, an ultra-durable material we’ve seen used on other racks. This attachment only weighs 15 pounds, making the VHS Lite a more user-friendly alternative than the full-sized VTS, which weighs in at 24 pounds. From a construction standpoint, we feel comfortable giving the VTS Lite 4 out of 5 stars.

In addition, we like that Bulletproof offers a wide range of options to accommodate different racks. You can choose between a 3” x 3” pair, a 2” x 3” pair, or a 2” x 2” pair. You also can choose different hook sizes based on the diameter of your barbell. This optionality, along with the added exercise variety you get from using the attachments, earns a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility.

Set to be released in May 2025, we’re excited to see this product in action. If you want a more streamlined solution than getting a standalone Smith machine, this is an attractive space- and money-saving solution. Based on the price and versatility, we give it a value rating of 4 out of 5 — though it could go higher once we get our hands on it.

As Smith machines have become more popular among the home gym community, we’ve ramped up our efforts to test ones from a variety of brands. This has allowed us to develop a thorough evaluation process that examines a number of key factors that impact your workout experience.

With options ranging from standard Smith machines to all-in-one trainers with cable machines, here’s what we assess during testing using a 1-5 scoring system:

What makes a Smith machine such a valuable training tool? If you’ve ever used one, you already know there’s added peace of mind knowing you have built-in support. Here’s an overview of the different benefits of utilizing this popular piece of equipment.

Unlike when you use a barbell and squat rack, the Smith machine provides a fixed bar path. This can help reduce the risk of injury and ensure a stable lifting environment.

“The Smith machine helps the athlete feel supported and gives them greater control and stability when performing an exercise,” says Mauro M. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness.

In particular, new lifters can benefit from starting out on a Smith machine so they can focus on their form while being supported by the machine.

“Maintaining correct form is important for avoiding injuries and maximizing the effectiveness of your workouts,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, PhD, RD. “Beginners might benefit from working with a personal trainer initially or taking a beginner class to learn proper techniques.”

The guided motion and added stability of a Smith machine makes it an ideal training tool for those returning from injury or anyone with mobility issues. It encourages proper form and can be a safer way to increase your strength and joint stability before moving on to free weights.

Maietta recommends starting with lighter weights to get a feel for the range of motion before progressing. “The fixed range of motion is not for everyone, so be sure to speak with your local fitness professional and listen to your body and joints if you feel any discomfort or pain during the planned movements,” he says.

If you prefer to work out alone or don’t have a training partner available, the Smith machine can act as a “spotter” for you. These machines offer an extra layer of safety, as you can easily rack the bar or set the safety spotters to a specific point that will keep you out of harm’s way.

In addition, this advantage allows you to safely follow progressive overload, a proven method for increasing muscle size and strength.

“This continual challenge helps your muscles grow stronger,” says Mohr. “It’s important to start with manageable increments to prevent injury.”

You won’t find many machines that offer as much versatility as the Smith machine. Want to train legs? You can knock out squat and lunge variations. Want to grow your chest and shoulders? Grab an adjustable weight bench and work on your bench press and overhead press without having to worry about keeping the bar stable. A high-end option like the Force USA G15 gives you the ability to perform cable exercises like cable crossovers, chest flys, and overhead triceps extensions.

“The Smith machine can be seen as the Swiss army knife of the weight room since it allows for several strength training exercises in its fixed vertical path, ranging from squats to overhead pressing movements,” says Maietta.

What should you consider when choosing a Smith machine? Based on our experience as equipment experts and dedicated lifters, here’s what we recommend:

Consider the machine’s footprint when determining if it is a good fit for your needs. One benefit of Smith machines is all-in-one trainers are available to consolidate the space needed for multiple workout stations.

Many of the home gym Smith machine options on this list are designed as all-in-one trainers designed to provide multiple workout functions with one convenient machine. The machine can include stations for a power rack, functional trainer, low-row attachment, chin-ups/pull-ups, dips, suspension trainers, and more.

Smith machines offer pulley systems with varying weight ratios, including 1:1 and 2:1. A 1:1 ratio means the weight you load is the exact weight you lift. A 2:1 ratio means you lift half of the weight you load. For instance, with a 2:1 ratio, if you load 100 pounds, you lift 50 pounds.

Some Force USA Smith machines, including the G15, allow users to easily switch between 2:1 and 4:1 ratios, which is helpful when people of various skills use the same machine.

Weight capacities vary depending on the functions offered by the machine. The weight capacities on this list start at 300 pounds. Be sure to confirm the machine’s weight capacity can accommodate your needs..

If you are looking for versatile strength-building home gym equipment to achieve a full-body workout, a Smith machine can help you achieve your goals. Since the 1950s, this game-changing machine has allowed gym-goers to work out safely without a spotter. Today, there is a wide range of consumer options, allowing you to experience the benefits of the Smith machine in the comfort of your own home gym.

Smith machines all perform similar functions, but there are different types of Smith machines available. For instance, some Smith machines provide a vertical path for motion, while other Smith machines provide a slightly angled path. Some Smith machines may be limited to the Smith machine function, while others are designed to be all-in-one machines with multiple stations for different exercises. Smith machines vary based on the manufacturer.

Yes, you can deadlift on a Smith machine, but whether you should depends on your skills and ability.Maietta suggests thinking through the following questions before performing moves on a Smith machine:-How is your range of motion?-Do you have the proper form or mobility to perform these compound moves?If you do not know, Maietta suggests working with a local fitness professional who will be able to help coach you and correct your form if necessary.

Yes, you can build muscle with the consistent use of a Smith machine. Smith machines are considered a good strength and muscle training option for beginners or those without a spotter. However, the drawback is motion is limited to a specific vertical (or slightly angled) path. For sports-specific muscle building, some experts prefer free weight exercises.

Yes, you can squat with a Smith machine. Safety features such as hooks and stoppers can help provide extra protection. Again, be mindful of your abilities and consult with a fitness pro if you are unsure of how to do this safely and with proper form.

Stephen is an ISSA-certified personal trainer and nutritionist with an immense passion for health and fitness. A two-time University of Florida graduate and longtime rugby player, he brings more than a decade of strength training experience, plus a diverse writing and editing background. When he’s not creating content or hitting the gym, he enjoys traveling, cooking, and attending music festivals around the world.

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Whether you know Robert Strauss for his work as “Robbie E” in TNA or more recently, “Robert Stone” as WWE’s General Manager of NXT, there’s no questioning this exciting performer’s work ethic. Fortunately, as the father of twin boys, and owner of several gyms in Florida, Stone is showing no signs of slowing down. And, at age 43, the “Dad Bod Destroyer” tells M&F how he’s evolved in order to hang with the next generation, both on screen and at home.

Formerly a physical education teacher, Robert Strauss made his pro wrestling debut in the year 2000 and soon worked preliminary matches for WWE until he signed a major deal with Total Nonstop Action in 2010, gaining fame as the charismatic “Robbie E.”  It was during his time in TNA that Strauss won a multitude of titles, including the promotion’s TV and X Division gold.

He also lifted the tag team belts on two occasions alongside Jessie Godderz, and in that team, known as “The BroMans,” the duo even received support from seven-time Mr Olympia, Phil Heath. Of course, Strauss is no stranger to Muscle & Fitness. In 2017, he became a popular contributor with his “Dad Bod Destroyer” workouts, detailing how he stayed in fighting shape while balancing life with his twin sons Cash and Carter, who were just months old as that point. In 2026, Strauss is still making a name for himself in the pro wrestling business, by keeping a tight leash on the young superstars of NXT, but while his current role involves a desk rather than a squared circle, Strauss is always ready for action.

As Robert Stone, the world traveled grappler has maintained his fitness and physique by evolving, to stay consistent. For example, as a young lion, he was able to throw around weights with the same reckless abandon that he showed to many a hapless foe inside the ring. But at 43, and juggling his now 10-year-old twins with a hectic role as NXT GM, coach at WWE’s Performance Center, and broadcast commentator to boot, Strauss has a busier schedule than ever despite the fact that he does not currently compete. Fortunately, the performer has combined his passion with his profession and also owns eight gyms across Florida — that’s five F45 and three FS8 studios—so he’s never stuck for a timely way to stay toned.

Because F45 workouts last no more than 45 minutes, Strauss is able to get great value from his sweat equity. “You’re able to get it all in,” he tells M&F, noting that following an efficient plan has cut down his workout time without sacrificing quality. “Sometimes there are days where I don’t have an hour and a half. I don’t have two hours to get in everything, if I want to stretch out, if I want to warm my body up,” adds Strauss, appreciating the fact that F45 sessions are already planned out and ready to go. “At 43, I do need to regularly warm my body up. So, the 45 minutes is clutch, to be able to just come in and leave, and everything be done.”

For mobility, Strauss shares that FS8 workouts focus on a lighter style of resistance training for improving mobility and maintaining longevity, while still building strength. That’s because FS8 sessions combine Pilates and yoga, with a major emphasis on the core as well as controlled, meaningful movements.

Because of his commitment to crushing each workout, Strauss still looks like he could step between the ropes at any moment, and he maintains a low level of bodyfat to stay ripped, but as a mature athlete, he prefers a sustainable approach to nutrition rather than the latest fads, and this means embracing the balance. “The thing is, I really know my body,” he explains. “Mentally, I want to enjoy things sometimes. I’m not always eating a strict, clean diet. I want to have a good time with my wife or my twins. If they want to get ice cream on the weekend, I’m going to get it too, if I want it.”

The clever coach says that allowing himself to indulge also provides him with the motivation to eat cleaner for the rest of the week. “It adds fuel to the fire for my next workout,” says Strauss. Still, this athlete is keen to avoid eating too late in the evenings and particularly avoids starchy carbs and processed sugars before he hits the hay.

Strauss refuses to rule out the possibility that Robert Stone could one day return him to the ring. He certainly would not be the oldest grappler on the roster if he did. Randy Orton and The Miz are 46, CM Punk is 48, and Rey Mysterio is 51. WWE fans also know that Stauss’s colleague and SmackDown General Manager, Nick Aldis, who is 39, returned for a one-off match against Gunther at SummerSlam 2026.

“If someone pushed me past the point where I need to step in the ring again, I don’t need a week to get ready,” says the authority of NXT. “I don’t need three months to get ready… I can be ready in an hour.”

#8586. The Peptide Door Is Cracking Open, Even If The Risks Aren’t Going Away

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Recently, an interesting thing happened. An athlete could read the World Anti-Doping Agency’s prohibited list and conclude that using certain peptides was a good way to lose a medal and win a ban. Then he could read a new federal announcement about those same compounds and conclude that Washington was opening the door to them. Same molecule. Two government-adjacent messages that seem to be saying two entirely different things. This could lead to quite a headache if you don’t bother reading the fine print.

On Oct. 30, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) published a draft interim policy involving six experimental peptides: BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, epitalon, and Semax. The idea is to use enforcement discretion while regulators decide whether these substances belong on the list of ingredients that certain licensed pharmacies and physicians can use in compounding. In plain English, HHS says it does not intend to pursue enforcement against qualifying compounders who follow a set of conditions. That is not the same thing as approving six new drugs.

Compounding is when a licensed professional prepares a medication for an individual patient rather than dispensing a mass-produced, approved product. The proposed policy calls for patient-specific prescriptions, traceable ingredients, quality documentation, reporting of serious adverse events, and other safeguards. It’s a long way from some internet chemist shipping you a vial labeled “research use only” with a complimentary discount code from a guy who benches four plates on Instagram.

I can see the argument for this. People are buying these things anyway. If a person is determined to use an experimental peptide, there’s an obvious appeal to getting it through a licensed professional instead of trusting an anonymous supplier whose laboratory might be a shack in a Chinese suburb. HHS says the policy is intended to steer people away from risky, unregulated sources. Fair enough. But a cleaner supply chain is not the same as a molecule that has been proven to work.

That’s the part the peptide evangelists tend to skip. BPC-157 has a reputation for repairing practically everything except a a broken heart. TB-500 gets talked about like it comes with replacement tendons in the box. But the clinical evidence supporting these sweeping claims in humans is thin. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) scientists raised concerns about the lack of convincing clinical data and about product safety.

An advisory committee nevertheless supported broader compounding access for six substances. Disagreement among experts is not proof that either side has discovered a miracle. But, the empirical data is unavoidably overwhelming. It’s a clear case of not believing the dyno numbers – the car feels faster. Such reports have dialed up to the point where the usual culprits smell dollar signs. However thin the clinical data, its being drowned out by an ever growing cadre of gym bros who swear it works, the list is prestigious too. Now all of a sudden the government tosses a glimmer of light down the hallway?  Out of nowhere? Isn’t it usually the government that’s slamming the door shut?

Note that the draft doesn’t authorize supplement companies to dump these compounds into pre-workouts and doesn’t establish that a product is safe or effective. The federal notice is open for public comment, and the policy can be revisited if safety or quality problems emerge. There are also state-level rules to contend with. Anyone announcing that peptides have been “FDA approved” has either misunderstood the document or is counting on you not reading it.

Now comes the part where competitive athletes have to pay close attention: BPC-157 and TB-500 remain prohibited under the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) rules used by many tested sports. A change in how federal regulators view compounding peptides does not rewrite the WADA rulebook. A prescription is not automatically permission to compete with a substance in your system.

The U.S. Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) has already sanctioned athletes over these compounds. Proof that the obstacle is here to stay.  What the outlaws will have to contend with is that while there are banned peptides that can already be detected directly in an athlete’s urine or blood, others present a much tougher analytical problem. And a ban doesn’t require WADA to have a practical routine test for the substance before they ban it. So, that right there is the loophole. And trust me when I tell you, it’s going to be exploited. Why? Because peptides work.

I’m all for serious research. I’m also for admitting when thousands of testimonials cannot all be wrong. If the new policy leads to better manufacturing controls and useful clinical data, good. If it merely replaces the sketchy online vial with a more expensive sketchy vial wearing a white coat, we haven’t accomplished much. There’s an important difference between making something easier to obtain and proving it’s worth obtaining. And if you compete in a tested sport, there’s a third question: whether using it costs you your career. Don’t confuse the three. And remember, if an athlete is prone to cheating, chances are he will cheat. And with what will he use to cheat? The stuff that works. Peptides are just now showing up in force and its a force to be reconned with.

On Episode 310 of The Menace Podcast, host Dennis James was joined by Milos Sarcev, Chris Cormier, and special guest Terrence Ruffin, and the conversation moved towards the 2027 Mr. Olympia final. The man they call “Ruff Diesel” talked to the panel about the progress he needs to make, to finally win a title at the Olympia.

Ruffin, an iconic Men’s Physique competitor has appeared in nine Olympia finals, and qualified for his tenth by securing victories at the Mexico and Slovakia Pro events in October. Ruffin was at ninth place at the ‘O’ in 2016 and 2018 but found a career high placing of second in 2020 and 2021. He came fifth in 2026, so what does he need to work on, in order to progress in 2027?

“Do you believe in your heart that you can still win the Olympia,” asked host Dennis James. “100%” came the quick response from Ruffin, who explained that despite his vast experience, he is still very excited about that prospect. Ruff Diesel then provided a glimpse into the adjustments he may need to make, if he is to dominate bodybuilding’s biggest stage.

“My biggest issue is, I always end up doing too much,” he explained. “I told myself, this year, I’m going to say no to a lot more stuff.” Ruffin shared that his constant travel and business interests could be spreading him too thin. “But I’m trying to not do so much,” he relented.

“But you’ve started a new business too,” challenged The Menace. “You’re prepping for the Olympia and you’re opening up a gym. I mean, come on.”

Ruffin agreed that he takes on a lot. “I’m even (going to) have a meeting with the gym tomorrow, about handing off a couple of things,” he said. “Just to make sure I can focus like I need to.”

Ruffin says that he has learned to appreciate that getting to the pinnacle of bodybuilding requires his complete attention. “I’m giving up a part of the business at the gym, so I don’t have to do, like, the day to day,” he explained. The competitor now intends to keep his diary clearer by turning down events and reducing his travel. “I’m just all in, on just the gym training, and all of that.”

With a renewed focus on the prize, Milos Sarcev pushed further on what progress Ruffin will need to make with his physique, in order to win. “Conditioning, or size?” asked The Mind. “Both,” answered Ruffin, with a smile.

To see this conversation in full on The Menace Podcast, where the panel also discussed the latest bodybuilding gossip, news, and results, check it out on the Muscle & Fitness YouTube channel.

The S&P 500 is an index that tracks the 500 largest publicly traded companies in the United States, weighted by market capitalization. It includes Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google), Meta, Berkshire Hathaway, and approximately 493 other companies that collectively represent about 80% of the total U.S. stock market value.

The index is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, which periodically adds and removes companies based on criteria including market cap (must exceed ~$18 billion), profitability, liquidity, and domicile. When a company is added to the S&P 500, every index fund tracking it automatically buys shares — and vice versa when companies are removed.

An S&P 500 index fund is a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds all 500 stocks in the same proportions as the index. Instead of picking individual stocks, you buy one fund and instantly own a piece of every major U.S. company. The fund mechanically replicates the index — no stock picking, no market timing, no overpaid fund managers.

The data is overwhelming. Over any 15-year period, approximately 92% of actively managed large-cap funds underperform the S&P 500 after fees, according to the SPIVA scorecard. Over 20 years, that number exceeds 95%. The reasons are simple: active fund managers charge 0.50% to 1.50% in annual fees, they generate taxable trading activity, and they cannot consistently pick winners.

Warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years. He won decisively — the index fund returned 125.8% vs 36.0% for the hedge fund basket. As Buffett has said: "By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most investment professionals."

The top S&P 500 index funds deliver nearly identical performance because they all track the same index. The differences come down to expense ratio, minimum investment, fund structure (ETF vs mutual fund), and tax efficiency. Here is a detailed comparison of the five most popular options.

The most popular S&P 500 ETF and the default recommendation for most FI seekers. At 0.03% expense ratio, a $500,000 investment costs just $150 per year in fees. VOO is tax-efficient due to the ETF structure and Vanguard's patented heartbeat trade process, which minimizes capital gains distributions. Fractional shares are available at most brokerages.

The lowest-cost S&P 500 fund available at 0.015% — half the cost of VOO. No minimum investment requirement makes it ideal for beginners. As a mutual fund, you can set up automatic investments in exact dollar amounts (e.g., $500/month). FXAIX is an excellent choice if your brokerage is Fidelity.

BlackRock's S&P 500 ETF with a 0.03% expense ratio, matching VOO. Functionally identical performance. Slightly different creation/redemption mechanics than VOO but the practical difference for individual investors is negligible. A strong alternative if you prefer iShares or trade through a brokerage that offers commission-free iShares ETFs.

The oldest and most heavily traded S&P 500 ETF, launched in 1993. SPY is the most liquid ETF in the world, making it the preferred choice for active traders. However, its 0.0945% expense ratio is over three times higher than VOO or IVV. For long-term FI investors, VOO or IVV are better choices. SPY's structure as a unit investment trust also makes it slightly less tax-efficient than VOO.

Schwab's mutual fund offering at 0.02% expense ratio with no minimum investment. Like FXAIX, the mutual fund structure allows automatic dollar-amount investing. An excellent choice for Schwab customers building automated investment plans.

Investing in an S&P 500 fund takes less than 15 minutes:

For retirement accounts (401k, IRA), look for the S&P 500 index fund option within your plan. It may have a different name (e.g., "Large Cap Index Fund" or "Institutional S&P 500") but will track the same index.

The total stock market index (tracked by VTI/VTSAX/FSKAX) holds approximately 3,600 stocks compared to the S&P 500's 500. The additional 3,100 stocks are mid-cap and small-cap companies. Here is how they compare:

Historically, the performance difference between the two is minimal — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year in either direction. The S&P 500 has outperformed in periods when large-cap growth stocks dominate. The total market has outperformed when small and mid-cap stocks lead. Over 20+ year periods, the returns converge closely.

The FI community's honest answer: it does not matter much which you choose. Investing $25,500 per year in VOO or VTI will produce nearly identical outcomes over 20 years. Consistency and contribution amount matter far more than the choice between S&P 500 and total market.

S&P 500 index funds typically yield 1.2% to 1.6% in annual dividends. In a tax-advantaged account (401k, IRA, Roth), dividends compound tax-free. In a taxable account, qualified dividends from S&P 500 funds are taxed at the favorable long-term capital gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

ETFs (VOO, IVV) are generally more tax-efficient than mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) in taxable accounts because ETFs rarely distribute capital gains. Vanguard's mutual funds are an exception — their patented ETF share class structure gives Vanguard mutual funds ETF-like tax efficiency. For taxable brokerage accounts, VOO or VFIAX (Vanguard's mutual fund version) are the most tax-efficient choices.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The most common mistake with S&P 500 index funds is waiting for the "right time" to invest. Research from Vanguard shows that investing a lump sum immediately outperforms dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time, because markets go up more often than they go down. Missing just the 10 best trading days over a 20-year period can cut your returns nearly in half. If you have money to invest, the data overwhelmingly says to invest it now — not next week, not after the next pullback, not when it "feels right."

Open an account at Vanguard (for VOO/VFIAX), Fidelity (for FXAIX), or Schwab (for SWPPX). All three offer commission-free trading on their own index funds, excellent customer service, and robust retirement account options. You can also buy any of these funds at most brokerages.

ETFs (VOO, IVV) trade like stocks at real-time prices and are more tax-efficient in taxable accounts. Mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) allow automatic dollar-amount investing and are better for set-it-and-forget-it contribution schedules. For retirement accounts, either works equally well.

Transfer cash to your brokerage account and buy your chosen fund. Start with whatever you have — there is no minimum too small. FXAIX and SWPPX have $0 minimums, and VOO can be purchased in fractional shares at most brokerages for as little as $1.

Automate monthly or per-paycheck contributions. This removes emotion from the process and ensures consistent dollar-cost averaging. Most brokerages let you schedule recurring purchases of mutual funds. For ETFs, some brokerages offer automatic ETF purchases as well.

If you hold other asset classes (bonds, international), rebalance once per year to maintain your target allocation. Otherwise, do nothing — do not check daily prices, do not sell during downturns, and do not chase performance. The S&P 500 has recovered from every crash in history. Time in the market beats timing the market.

Fidelity 500 Index Fund (FXAIX) has the lowest expense ratio at 0.015%. Schwab S&P 500 Index Fund (SWPPX) is next at 0.02%. VOO and IVV tie at 0.03%. All four are excellent — the fee difference between FXAIX (0.015%) and VOO (0.03%) on a $500,000 portfolio is just $75 per year. Choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage.

VOO is better for long-term investors. It charges 0.03% vs SPY's 0.0945%, saving you about $325 per year on a $500,000 portfolio. VOO is also more tax-efficient due to its ETF share class structure. SPY's advantage is liquidity for active trading, which long-term index investors do not need. For buy-and-hold FI investing, VOO is the clear winner.

Either is an excellent choice. The S&P 500 covers approximately 80% of the U.S. stock market by value. A total market fund adds mid-cap and small-cap stocks for fuller diversification. Over long periods, performance is nearly identical — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year. The FI community consensus is that the best fund is the one you will consistently invest in without overthinking the decision.

As little as $1. FXAIX and SWPPX have zero minimum investments. VOO and IVV can be purchased as fractional shares at most brokerages. There is no minimum too small — starting with $50 or $100 per month and increasing contributions as your income grows is exactly how most people on the FI path begin.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10.3% per year on average since 1957 (including dividends). Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7.0% per year. These are long-term averages — individual years range from -38% (2008) to +38% (1995). The key is staying invested through the down years to capture the recovery gains that follow.

S&P 500 index funds carry market risk — they can lose significant value in the short term (the index dropped 34% in early 2020 and 38% in 2008). However, the S&P 500 has recovered from every decline in its history and has never lost money over any 20-year period. For investors with a 10+ year time horizon, the risk of not investing (missing out on 10% average annual returns) is far greater than the risk of temporary market declines.

S&P 500 index funds are the single most important building block for long-term wealth. With expense ratios as low as 0.015%, you keep virtually all of your returns while owning a piece of the 500 largest U.S. companies. VOO, FXAIX, IVV, and SWPPX all deliver near-identical performance — choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage and automate your contributions. The FI community has proven through thousands of real-world examples that consistent investing in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, held for decades without panic selling, is the most reliable path to building wealth and reaching financial independence.

#8580. Joe Baena Gave Fans a Glimpse of His Bodybuilding Debut

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Joe Baena may be the son of Arnold Schwarzenegger, but he is certainly forging his own path in the competitive bodybuilding business. The 29-year-old recently made his debut at the INBA PNBA World Cup in El Segundo, CA, reaching an impressive fifth place on the natural stage. And, for anyone who is aspiring to compete in the future, Baena chronicled his first pro outing for an insightful glimpse.

“Each photo has a great story of what it is like to be a competitor at a bodybuilding show,” posted Baena for his 895,000 Instagram followers, providing all the backstage goings on during the World Cup on November 7.

Earlier this year, the young upstart dominated in the Men’s Physique category of the NPC Classic Physique and Open, during his amateur debut, and then went to earn his pro card at the INBA Iron Gladiator event a week later on April 4.

Sharing his feelings as he arrived for the World Cup, Baena said, “Tan on, nerves high, and just trying to mentally prepare for the day ahead. Excited to see the carbs doing their work and that the abs are still there after two meals.”

Sharing an image of the changing room, Baena explained that before each competitor gets under the spotlight, they like to watch the other athletes first. “Seeing the guys in the other classes is always very exciting,” he wrote. “As you can see new things in their posing routines and styles. Everyone brings their individual personalities to the stage.”

Half an hour before his own routine, Baena began to carb up. “About 20 to 30 minutes before stepping on the stage, I’m getting my last light carbs in to fill up the muscles and look as pumped as possible,” he shared. “A couple rice cakes and a little honey drizzle does just the trick.”

Then comes “The Pump Up” to get the blood flowing into the muscles. “There’s no gym or equipment provided for most bodybuilding competitions, so you have to bring your own resistance bands or get some help from another competitor backstage,” explained Baena. “The camaraderie was amazing and everyone was just so excited to be there.”

For this detailed prepper, being specific about which muscles to pump is highly important. “You gotta make sure you pump up the right muscles, especially the ones that are lacking or need the most volume to present,” he shared. “For me, I know my arms aren’t the biggest, so I always put a little extra effort into pumping up the biceps and triceps.”

“The first thing when you step out on stage is you all lineup and basically square up next to each other,” said the competitor. “Presenting yourself in the best way possible is important along with standing out from the other competitors. After you’ve all lined up and done the mandatory poses it’s time for the pose down! You all get as close to the judges as possible and flex off together. Standing next to each other, hitting all your favorite poses and trying to present yourself as the largest, most ripped and best-looking competitor out there. Occasionally going pose for pose or just doing your own thing, you want to attract the judge’s attention as much as possible.”

The posing routine is the “last but definitely not least” aspect of the competition, wrote Baena. “The posing routine is my favorite part of the whole process. The artistry aspect of bodybuilding is what I think makes the sport so great. Building your body up to be statue-like and choreographing a routine that emulates and shows the aesthetic and beauty of the body.”

Having flexed for all that he was worth at the World Cup, Baena explained that with 11 competitors in his category, “It was extremely nerve-racking, standing there waiting for my name to get called out. My goal going into the show was to get into the top five so when I heard my name get called at fifth place it was a huge relief. I achieved what I signed out for and could finally think forward about getting a burger. Of course, the dream is to win the show and be the number one overall, but it all comes in due time and with the right amount of work. This was only my first pro show, and I couldn’t be more proud of myself. This is my first year competing with my first show being the end of March, the second show been the week after, and this being only my third show. A lot of the guys I competed with have been competing for many years now, so it is great motivation to be able to stand up and stack up next to them.”

Finally, Baena indulges in a well-earned meal. But what did he eat? “The Apple Pan,” he revealed. “Definitely one of the best burgers in LA. Had to celebrate at the Apple Pan for my first meal post competition. I ordered two burgers and two slices of pie. Somehow, even after eating all that I still had room for more.”

Glowing after “The Champion’s Pie,” Baena said, “I’m a huge pie lover and having been on prep during many weddings, my birthday, and other celebrations (where) I had to skip on many desserts, this pie tasted incredible, but I will say achieving a goal you set out for is a lot sweeter than any cheat meal.”

And that’s just as well, because soon begins the prep for Baena’s next competition.
